subject: Calculating ESW for a covariate level

messages.author: 06199470668a2843
messages.subject: Calculating ESW for a covariate level
parts:
Hello all,

I am experiencing some difficulties in manually calculating effective
strip widths for selected covariate levels in a MCDS analysis. I think my
methods follow exactly the directions given in the online help, yet the
results don't seem to fit.
I have calculated realistic-seeming estimates for some of my models, but
now I've come upon one where my constructed estimates are not even in the
ballpark of the program's ESW estimate, which makes me wonder if I
mishandled the other ones as well.

The model that gives me pause is this:

##########################

Effort : 30921.00 # samples : 65
Width : 78.00000 Left : 0.0000000
# observations: 49

Model
Half-normal key, k(y) =3D Exp(-y**2/(2*s**2))

s =3D A(1) * Exp(fcn(A(2)) + fcn(A(3)) + fcn(A(4)))
Parameter A(1) is the intercept of the scale parameter s.
Parameter A(2) is the coefficient of level BREED of factor covariate T=
OY.
Parameter A(3) is the coefficient of level POST of factor covariate TO=
Y.
Parameter A(4) is the coefficient of covariate FROM SUNRISE.


Point Standard Percent Coef. 95 Percent
Parameter Estimate Error of Variation Confidence Interv=
al
--------- ----------- ----------- -------------- -------------------=
---
A( 1) 3.917 4.407
A( 2) 0.3933 0.9132
A( 3) -0.3730 0.5553
A( 4) 0.9323E-02 0.6276E-02
f(0) 0.21287E-01 0.37605E-02 17.67 0.14955E-01=20
0.30301E-01
p 0.60226 0.10639 17.67 0.42311 0.857=
27
ESW 46.976 8.2985 17.67 33.002 66.8=
67


####################

This model uses two covariates: factor covariate "TOY" (time of year) wit=
h
three levels winter, breed, and post, and a continuous covariate "minutes
since sunrise".
I want to calculate ESWs for the levels of TOY. My understanding of the
method is: 1) calculate sigma for the particular covariate level, which
would be A(1) for WINTER [3.92], A(1)*exp(A(2)) for BREED [5.8] or
A(1)*exp(A(3)) for POST [2.7]
2) plug the sigma into the key function, then integrate the key function
for the interval 0 -> truncation distance (I am using the S-PLUS function
"integrate" for this)

The resulting values are 4.91, 7.26, and 3.38 - extremely small ESWs!
If it is indeed the case that the ESW estimate for each of the covariate
levels results in such small values, how does Distance arrive at an
overall ESW estimate of 46.976? I am not sure how to approach replicatin=
g
this full model estimate, either - evidently that would not just consist
of using a sigma with all four coefficients activated?

I am aware that the number of sightings is on the low side, and so might
not use this particular data subset. My suspicion is that what I am seein=
g
might be a result of forcing too many parameters on a poor data set size,
but some insight into this would still be very valuable to check whether =
I
am doing the right thing with my other models!

Hope someone can shed some light on this
best regards
florian

--=20

messages.author: 5140016d70f6ba82
messages.subject: Re: Calculating ESW for a covariate level
parts:
If I understood what you wrote, the values you computed were for 0
minutes from sunrise. The average ESW is based on the set of observed
minutes from sunrise with the set of factor levels.

You may want to try a model without the continuous covariate so you can
see more easily how it works.

--jeff
